[Page 1] Output-Based Education (OBE) Outcome
[Page 1] Initial Group Brainstorming and Proposed Project Plan
[Page 1] Course and Section: ____________________
[Page 1] Group Number: ____________________
[Page 1] Date: October 16, 2026
[Page 1] Group Members
[Page 1] 1. Gjia
[Page 1] 2. Angel
[Page 1] 3. Jeff
[Page 1] 4. Dinesse
[Page 1] I. Group Topic Brainstorming
[Page 1] During our brainstorming, each of us suggested a social issue that we believe is relevant to the
[Page 1] Philippines today and can be connected to the life or writings of Dr. José Rizal. We also
[Page 1] considered whether we could make a simple and practical social action project about each topic.
[Page 1] 1. Gjia
[Page 1] Proposed Topic: "The Price of Being Poor": How Small Financial Barriers Create Bigger
[Page 1] Inequality
[Page 1] • Even small expenses for transportation, documents, school requirements, or basic services can
[Page 1] be difficult for families with limited income.
[Page 1] • In El Filibusterismo, Cabesang Tales experiences land-related injustice and financial
[Page 1] hardship. His story shows how unfair systems can make life harder for ordinary people.
[Page 1] • We think this topic is important because small costs can add up and prevent people from
[Page 1] accessing opportunities.
[Page 1] • A possible project would be to prepare easy-to-follow guides about available school
[Page 1] assistance or public services and their requirements.
[Page 1] 2. Angel
[Page 1] Proposed Topic: "From Friars to Influencers": Blind Obedience to Powerful Personalities
[Page 1] • Some people easily trust statements from influencers, celebrities, or powerful figures without
[Page 1] checking the information.
[Page 1] • In Noli Me Tangere, Padre Damaso and Padre Salvi show how powerful people can influence
[Page 1] the beliefs and decisions of others.
[Page 1] • We think students should learn to question claims respectfully and look for evidence instead
[Page 1] of believing something only because a popular person said it.
[Page 1] • A possible project would be a discussion and simple activity about checking claims made by
[Page 1] influential people.
[Page 2] 3. Jeff
[Page 2] Proposed Topic: "Viral ang Isyu, Tahimik ang Aksyon": Performative Activism
[Page 2] • We often see social issues go viral. People may share posts or react online, but we want to
[Page 2] know whether online awareness also leads to real involvement.
[Page 2] • In Noli Me Tangere, Ibarra tries to help his community by establishing a school. In El
[Page 2] Filibusterismo, Isagani and other students work together to push for educational reform.
[Page 2] • Rizal also taught students and helped his community while living in Dapitan. These examples
[Page 2] remind us that concern for others can lead to practical action.
[Page 2] • A possible project would be to encourage students to join one simple volunteer activity, using
[Page 2] social media to invite and organize participants.
[Page 2] 4. Dinesse
[Page 2] Proposed Topic: "Guilty Before Proven Innocent": Trial by Social Media
[Page 2] • People can be judged or criticized online before the full story or evidence is known.
[Page 2] • In Noli Me Tangere, Ibarra is linked to an uprising and suffers from accusations. In El
[Page 2] Filibusterismo, students face suspicion after the pasquinades incident.
[Page 2] • This is relevant today because online accusations can damage reputations, even before the
[Page 2] facts are checked.
[Page 2] • A possible project would be a student workshop about fair judgment, responsible posting, and
[Page 2] checking facts.
[Page 2] II. Our Chosen Topic
[Page 2] Selected Topic: "Viral ang Isyu, Tahimik ang Aksyon": Performative Activism (Jeff's
[Page 2] suggestion)
[Page 2] After discussing our four choices, we decided to choose Jeff's topic on performative activism. We
[Page 2] chose it because we can relate to it as students who use social media almost every day. We often
[Page 2] see people, including ourselves, sharing or reacting to posts about social issues. We want to find
[Page 2] out how this awareness can encourage us to do something helpful in our community.
[Page 2] We do not believe that sharing posts is always a bad thing. Online advocacy can spread
[Page 2] information, encourage donations, and invite volunteers. We also understand that not everyone has
[Page 2] the time or money to join activities. Our focus is not to judge people, but to help students find
[Page 2] realistic ways to take part.
[Page 2] We see a connection to Rizal's works because Ibarra tried to build a school and the students in El
[Page 2] Filibusterismo worked together for reform. Rizal's service in Dapitan also shows how we can help
[Page 2] others through simple, useful actions. This topic fits our project because we can survey students,
[Page 2] organize a small volunteer activity, and evaluate what we learned.
[Page 2] Proposed Project Title: From Posts to Purpose: Turning Online Awareness into Real Community
[Page 2] Action
[Page 2] Our project title, participants, and activities are still subject to group discussion and approval.
[Page 3] III. Initial Situation Analysis
[Page 3] A. What Is the Issue?
[Page 3] Performative activism happens when someone publicly shows support for a cause mainly to look
[Page 3] concerned or gain approval, without genuine interest in helping that cause. However, we cannot
[Page 3] judge a person's intentions from one post alone. Sharing accurate information can also be a useful
[Page 3] form of activism.
[Page 3] Our group wants to study the gap between being aware of social issues online and having the
[Page 3] chance to take meaningful action. We will focus on college students and the practical things that
[Page 3] may help them participate.
[Page 3] B. Why Does It Happen?
[Page 3] Some possible reasons are:
[Page 3] • Students may be busy with schoolwork or family responsibilities.
[Page 3] • Some volunteer activities require transportation money, time, or other resources.
[Page 3] • Students may not know where to find safe and trustworthy volunteer opportunities.
[Page 3] • Trending posts and online reactions can sometimes receive more attention than follow-up
[Page 3] activities.
[Page 3] • Some people may want to help but do not know where to start.
[Page 3] We will not assume these reasons are true for everyone. We plan to ask students about their
[Page 3] experiences and look for reliable studies about youth activism.
[Page 3] C. Who May Be Affected?
[Page 3] Our possible participants are college students from our school or a nearby student organization. A
[Page 3] partner community may also benefit if we organize a volunteer activity based on a need they
[Page 3] identify.
[Page 3] If awareness does not lead to opportunities for participation, students may miss chances to
[Page 3] contribute and learn through service. However, we also recognize that online sharing can be
[Page 3] useful, especially for people who cannot join activities in person.
[Page 3] D. What Can We Do About It?
[Page 3] We can start by asking students how they engage with social issues, what prevents them from
[Page 3] volunteering, and what simple activities they would consider joining. We can hold a short
[Page 3] discussion about meaningful action and invite them to one manageable community activity, if a
[Page 3] school or community partner approves it.
[Page 3] We will use reliable references about youth activism, and we will review the relevant events in
[Page 3] Rizal's novels. Our goal is to connect awareness with action, not to criticize students who have
[Page 3] limited time or resources.
[Page 4] IV. Connection to Rizal
[Page 4] A. Noli Me Tangere
[Page 4] Crisostomo Ibarra plans to establish a school because he believes education can improve his
[Page 4] community. This connects to our project because he tries to turn an idea into something useful. We
[Page 4] want students to see that caring about a problem can be a starting point for small, practical actions.
[Page 4] B. El Filibusterismo
[Page 4] Isagani, Makaraig, and other students work together to request a Spanish-language academy.
[Page 4] Although their effort faces resistance, their story shows young people organizing around an issue
[Page 4] that matters to them. We can learn from their willingness to participate and cooperate.
[Page 4] C. Rizalian Values We Can Apply
[Page 4] • Education: We should understand an issue before deciding how to help.
[Page 4] • Responsibility: We should be sincere and careful about the causes we support.
[Page 4] • Cooperation: We can do more when we work with others.
[Page 4] • Service: We can use our time and skills to help our community.
[Page 4] • Love of country: Small actions that serve others are one way of showing concern for our
[Page 4] society.
[Page 4] Rizal did not write about social media or performative activism. We are applying the lessons from
[Page 4] his novels, together with his work in Dapitan, to an issue we experience today.
[Page 4] V. Possible Social Action Project
[Page 4] From Posts to Purpose: Turning Online Awareness into Real Community Action
[Page 4] Main Goal: To encourage students to turn their awareness of social issues into simple and
[Page 4] meaningful community participation.
[Page 4] Our group is considering the following activities:
[Page 4] 1. Quick Student Survey - Ask around 30-50 willing students how they support causes online,
[Page 4] whether they have volunteered, and what makes participation difficult.
[Page 4] 2. From Posts to Purpose Discussion - Hold a short conversation about useful online advocacy,
[Page 4] volunteer opportunities, and Rizal's example of service.
[Page 4] 3. One Small Action Challenge - Invite students to sign up for one low-cost activity based on a
[Page 4] need identified by a partner school or community.
[Page 4] 4. Community Volunteer Activity - Carry out the chosen activity, such as a supervised cleanup
[Page 4] and proper waste segregation, with permission and guidance.
[Page 4] 5. Feedback and Reflection - Ask participants what they learned, record actual participation, and
[Page 4] discuss how they could join future activities.
[Page 4] These are initial suggestions. We will choose the final community activity based on what our
[Page 4] partner actually needs and what we can safely and realistically do.
[Page 5] VI. Initial Action Plan

[Page 5] Possible resources: Mobile phones, free online survey forms, internet access, presentation
[Page 5] materials, drinking water, and basic activity supplies if needed.
[Page 5] Possible partners: Faculty adviser, student organizations, school offices, or a barangay
[Page 5] representative, depending on availability and permission.
[Page 5] VII. Sustainability and Responsible Implementation
[Page 5] To help our project remain practical and useful, we may:
[Page 5] • Use free online tools and keep the activity small to avoid unnecessary expenses.
[Page 5] • Coordinate with an existing student organization or community partner rather than starting a
[Page 5] new program that we cannot maintain.
[Page 5] • Choose an activity based on an actual community need and obtain permission before
[Page 5] conducting it.
[Page 5] • Respect participants' privacy, ask for consent before taking or sharing photos, and avoid
[Page 5] judging anyone who cannot volunteer.
[Page 5] • Share a simple guide on how students can join similar activities after our project ends.
[Page 5] • Use attendance, a short feedback form, and partner feedback to check what our project
[Page 5] actually achieved.
[Page 5] We know that one event will not solve a major social issue or prove a lasting change in behavior.
[Page 5] Still, we hope that our project can give students an easy first step toward volunteering and show
[Page 5] that social media can be used to organize helpful actions.
[Page 5] Inspired by Ibarra, the student reformers in El Filibusterismo, and Rizal's work in Dapitan, we
[Page 5] want to remind ourselves that we can begin helping our community through small, realistic efforts.
